title: Pointers to Pointers
summary: A pointer is a variable, so it has an address too, and a pointer can hold that address. A **pointer to a pointer** lets a function change which object another pointer points at, and it is how arrays of pointers, command-line arguments and many Windows API "out" parameters work.
markdown:
## A pointer is just another variable Lesson 1.03 showed that a pointer is a variable holding an address. Like every variable, the pointer itself lives somewhere in memory and has an address of its own. Nothing stops you storing **that** address in another variable: ```cpp #include int main() { int gold{ 250 }; int* p{ &gold }; // p holds the address of gold int** pp{ &p }; // pp holds the address of p std::cout << "gold = " << gold << '\n'; std::cout << "*p = " << *p << '\n'; std::cout << "**pp = " << **pp << '\n'; **pp = 300; // follow pp to p, follow p to gold, write there std::cout << "gold = " << gold << '\n'; return 0; } ``` ``` gold = 250 *p = 250 **pp = 250 gold = 300 ``` Read the types from the right: `int**` is a pointer to (a pointer to an int). Each `*` in an expression follows one arrow. ```mermaid flowchart LR PP["pp
holds &p"] -->|"*pp"| P["p
holds &gold"] P -->|"*p, or **pp"| G["gold
250"] ``` | Expression | Type | Means | |---|---|---| | `pp` | `int**` | The address of `p` | | `*pp` | `int*` | The value of `p`: the address of `gold` | | `**pp` | `int` | The value of `gold` | In memory, all three are just numbers in boxes: `pp`'s 8 bytes hold `p`'s address, `p`'s 8 bytes hold `gold`'s address, and `gold`'s 4 bytes hold 250. ## Why you would want one: changing someone else's pointer A function receives copies of its arguments. Pass it a pointer and it can change the thing pointed at, but not the caller's pointer itself. To change the caller's pointer, the function needs that pointer's address. ```cpp #include struct Enemy { const char* name; int health; }; // Makes *target point at the weakest living enemy, or nullptr if none are alive. void pickWeakest(Enemy* enemies, int count, Enemy** target) { *target = nullptr; for (int i{ 0 }; i < count; ++i) { Enemy* e{ &enemies[i] }; if (e->health > 0 && (*target == nullptr || e->health < (*target)->health)) *target = e; } } int main() { Enemy pack[]{ { "wolf", 30 }, { "bat", 0 }, { "rat", 12 } }; Enemy* aim{ nullptr }; pickWeakest(pack, 3, &aim); std::cout << "aiming at the " << aim->name << '\n'; return 0; } ``` ``` aiming at the rat ``` `pickWeakest` writes into `*target`, which is the caller's `aim`. This "out parameter" style is everywhere in C and in the Windows API, where functions return an error code and hand back the object they created through a pointer to your pointer. Chapter 5 is full of calls like this: ```cpp // The function writes the new object's address into iface. IUnknown* iface{ nullptr }; HRESULT hr{ CreateSomething(IID_PPV_ARGS(&iface)) }; ``` In modern C++ code you would more often return the pointer, or pass `Enemy*&` (a reference to a pointer, lesson 3.03). But you need to read the `**` form fluently. ## Arrays of pointers The other common use is an array whose elements are pointers. `main` can receive the program's command-line arguments that way: ```cpp #include int main(int argc, char** argv) { // argv points at an array of argc pointers, each pointing at one argument's characters. std::cout << "argc = " << argc << '\n'; for (int i{ 1 }; i < argc; ++i) std::cout << "argument " << i << ": " << argv[i] << '\n'; return 0; } ``` Run with `game.exe --level 3`, `argv[0]` is the program's path, `argv[1]` points at `"--level"` and `argv[2]` at `"3"`. `argv[1][2]` is `'l'`: index into the array of pointers, then into the characters. ``` argv ──▶ ┌─────────┐ │ argv[0] │──▶ "C:\games\game.exe" ├─────────┤ │ argv[1] │──▶ "--level" ├─────────┤ │ argv[2] │──▶ "3" ├─────────┤ │ nullptr │ └─────────┘ ``` Arrays of pointers also let you sort or reorder large objects cheaply: shuffle 8-byte pointers instead of copying the objects. ## Pointer arithmetic still works one level down `argv + 1` moves along the array of pointers by one pointer (8 bytes). `*(argv + 1) + 2` moves along the characters of the second argument by two characters. Each level has its own element size, and pointer arithmetic always uses the size of the thing pointed at. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Passing the pointer when the function needs its address > `pickWeakest(pack, 3, aim)` does not compile, which is good. With `void*` parameters it might, and then the function writes over the wrong thing. Match the number of `*`s. > [!warning] Forgetting the parentheses in `(*target)->health` > `*target->health` means `*(target->health)`, which is something else entirely. > [!warning] Following a null pointer at either level > Check `pp` before `*pp`, and `*pp` before `**pp`. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What does a pointer to a pointer hold? - The value of the object at the end of the chain + The address of another pointer variable - Two addresses, one for each level - The address of the first element of an array > An `int**` holds the address of an `int*`. Dereference it once to get that pointer, twice to get the `int`. ? Give two common reasons to use a pointer to a pointer. - To make code run faster, and to save memory - To point at a function, and to point at a member + To let a function re-aim the caller's pointer, and for arrays of pointers - To avoid null checks, and to make a pointer constant > A function given an `Enemy*` can only change the enemy; given an `Enemy**` it can change which enemy the caller's pointer refers to. ? How many bytes does `argv + 1` move on x64? + Eight, the size of one pointer - One, because `argv` holds characters - Four, the size of an `int` - It depends on how long the first argument is > Pointer arithmetic moves by the size of the thing pointed at, and `argv` points at `char*` pointers, which are 8 bytes on x64. ? `int x{ 5 }; int* p{ &x }; int** pp{ &p };` What is the type of `*pp`? - `int` + `int*` - `int**` > One `*` removes one level: `*pp` is `p`, an `int*`. ? Why does a function need an `Enemy**` parameter to change which enemy the caller's `Enemy*` points at? - Pointers cannot be passed to functions + It needs the caller's pointer's address to write into it - `Enemy*` parameters are read-only > Arguments are copies. To change the caller's variable, a function needs its address, and here the variable is itself a pointer. ? In `int main(int argc, char** argv)`, what is `argv[2][0]`? - The third character of the first argument - The number of arguments + The first character of the third command-line argument > `argv[2]` is the third pointer in the array; `[0]` takes the first character it points at. ```
ideas:
- In Visual Studio, set **Project Properties → Debugging → Command Arguments** to `--level 3 --hard` and run the `argv` example.
- Change `pickWeakest` to take `Enemy*& target` instead of `Enemy** target`. What has to change in the body and in the call?
- Add `int*** ppp{ &pp };` to the first example and change `gold` through it.

cards.q: What does a pointer to a pointer hold?
cards.a:
The address of another pointer variable

An `int**` holds the address of an `int*`. Dereference it once to get that pointer, twice to get the `int`.

cards.q: Give two common reasons to use a pointer to a pointer.
cards.a:
To let a function re-aim the caller's pointer, and for arrays of pointers

A function given an `Enemy*` can only change the enemy; given an `Enemy**` it can change which enemy the caller's pointer refers to.

cards.q: How many bytes does `argv + 1` move on x64?
cards.a:
Eight, the size of one pointer

Pointer arithmetic moves by the size of the thing pointed at, and `argv` points at `char*` pointers, which are 8 bytes on x64.

cards.q: `int x{ 5 }; int* p{ &x }; int** pp{ &p };` What is the type of `*pp`?
cards.a:
`int*`

One `*` removes one level: `*pp` is `p`, an `int*`.

cards.q: Why does a function need an `Enemy**` parameter to change which enemy the caller's `Enemy*` points at?
cards.a:
It needs the caller's pointer's address to write into it

Arguments are copies. To change the caller's variable, a function needs its address, and here the variable is itself a pointer.

cards.q: In `int main(int argc, char** argv)`, what is `argv[2][0]`?
cards.a:
The first character of the third command-line argument

`argv[2]` is the third pointer in the array; `[0]` takes the first character it points at.
